questions.stem: What is the main purpose of an acid-base titration?

options.text: To find how much alkali exactly neutralises a measured quantity of acid
options.explanation: Quantifying the neutralisation is the core purpose, and from it follow moles, concentrations and volumes.

options.text: To make the acid and alkali stronger
options.explanation: Nothing is concentrated by titrating; the method measures how much reacts.

options.text: To heat the solutions gently
options.explanation: No heating is involved in a titration at all.

options.text: To check the colour of the solutions
options.explanation: Colour is only watched through the indicator; the purpose is the measurement.

questions.stem: Which piece of apparatus delivers the variable volume during a titration?

options.text: The burette
options.explanation: The burette is filled with acid and run in gradually, giving the variable volume that is recorded before and after.

options.text: The pipette
options.explanation: The pipette delivers one fixed volume, 25 cm3 of alkali here, into the flask.

options.text: The conical flask
options.explanation: The flask holds the reaction mixture; it measures nothing.
options.misconception: container mistaken for a measuring tool

options.text: The white tile
options.explanation: The tile only improves visibility of the colour change.
options.misconception: supporting item given a measuring role

questions.stem: What is the pipette used for in this titration?

options.text: Placing exactly 25 cm3 of sodium hydroxide solution into the conical flask
options.explanation: The pipette and filler deliver one precise, fixed volume to start the titration.

options.text: Adding the indicator drop by drop
options.explanation: Indicator drops are added straight from a bottle; the pipette handles the alkali volume.

options.text: Measuring the gas released
options.explanation: No gas is measured in an acid-alkali titration.

options.text: Stirring the mixture during the titration
options.explanation: Swirling the flask does the mixing; the pipette is for measuring.

questions.stem: Besides quantifying neutralisation, what can titrations be used to prepare?

options.text: Salts, made under carefully controlled reacting volumes
options.explanation: The note lists salt preparation as another use of titrations.

options.text: New elements
options.explanation: Titrations rearrange ions in solution; they never create elements.

options.text: Pure metals by electrolysis
options.explanation: Electrolysis is a separate process; titration is a volumetric method.

options.text: Indicators from plants
options.explanation: Indicators are extracted from plants directly; titrations consume them, not make them.

questions.stem: Which quantities can a titration result help you calculate?

options.text: Moles, concentration and volume
options.explanation: These are exactly the quantities the note says may be asked for.

options.text: Mass of the apparatus only
options.explanation: Weighing apparatus is irrelevant to titration calculations.

options.text: Temperature change of the mixture
options.explanation: That belongs to calorimetry, not titration.

options.text: Colour intensity only
options.explanation: Colour is qualitative; the calculation targets are the three listed quantities.

questions.stem: What property of a solution does a titration analyse?
questions.modelAnswer: Its concentration — a titration is a method of analysing the concentration of solutions.

questions.stem: Name the three centre-piece pieces of apparatus in a titration setup.
questions.modelAnswer: A burette, a pipette and a conical flask.

questions.stem: Explain why a titration can prepare a salt as cleanly as it measures neutralisation.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a titration finds exactly how much alkali neutralises a quantity of acid; repeating that neutralisation at the measured, controlled volumes lets the salt be prepared with no leftover acid or alkali.

questions.stem: A titration finds the volume of hydrochloric acid that neutralises a measured alkali sample. State the three quantities this kind of result is used to calculate in exam questions.
questions.modelAnswer: The moles present, the concentration of one of the solutions, or the volume needed for neutralisation — moles, concentration and volume are the three calculation targets.

questions.stem: Why is a little acid run through the burette before you start?

options.text: To remove air bubbles, which collect in the jet space below the tap
options.explanation: A bubble in the jet space would later escape and falsify the volume delivered, so it is flushed out first.

options.text: To warm the burette to room temperature
options.explanation: Temperature plays no part; the flush targets bubbles.

options.text: To clean the burette of all acid traces
options.explanation: The burette is already filled with that acid; the small run clears the jet space specifically.

options.text: To check the tap still turns
options.explanation: A tap check is sensible but is not the stated purpose; bubbles are.

questions.stem: To what precision should burette readings be recorded?

options.text: To the nearest 0.05 cm3
options.explanation: Both the starting point and the final titre are recorded to 0.05 cm3.

options.text: To the nearest whole cm3
options.explanation: Whole cm3 would waste the burette's precision and spoil the concordance test.

options.text: To the nearest 5 cm3
options.explanation: That is far too coarse for titration work.

options.text: Precision does not matter if the colour change is sharp
options.explanation: A sharp endpoint still needs precisely recorded volumes to be useful.

questions.stem: What is the white tile under the conical flask for?

options.text: It makes the indicator's colour changes more obvious
options.explanation: Against a white background the endpoint colour flip is far easier to see.

options.text: It keeps the flask warm
options.explanation: No warming is wanted; the tile is about visibility.

options.text: It stops the flask from tipping over
options.explanation: Stability is incidental; the stated purpose is seeing the colour change.

options.text: It absorbs any spilled acid
options.explanation: Spill control is not the tile's stated job.

questions.stem: Two titres of 14.90 cm3 and 15.00 cm3 are obtained. What can be said about them?

options.text: They are concordant, because they lie within 0.1 cm3 of each other
options.explanation: The difference is exactly 0.1 cm3, meeting the concordance rule, so both results count.

options.text: They are discordant and both must be discarded
options.explanation: Results within 0.1 cm3 are concordant and are kept, not discarded.

options.text: Only the larger value may be used
options.explanation: Concordant results are averaged, not cherry-picked.

options.text: The rough titre should be included in the mean
options.explanation: The rough run is always left out; the mean uses the concordant pair.

questions.stem: Why must the funnel be removed from the burette before titrating?

options.text: Drips from the funnel would fall into the burette and falsify the initial reading
options.explanation: A late drip adds volume you never recorded, which corrupts the titre.

options.text: The funnel would react with the acid
options.explanation: Funnels are inert in this context; the problem is stray drips, not reaction.

options.text: The funnel blocks the jet space
options.explanation: The jet space is below the tap; the funnel sits at the top.

options.text: It is only a matter of tidiness
options.explanation: Tidiness is not the issue; measurement integrity is.

questions.stem: What must be flushed out of the burette's jet space before the first reading is taken?
questions.modelAnswer: Air bubbles — a little acid is run through first to clear the jet space between the tap and the tip.

questions.stem: How finely must each burette reading be recorded?
questions.modelAnswer: To the nearest 0.05 cm3, read at eye level.

questions.stem: Explain why the acid is added one drop at a time only near the endpoint, even though larger portions were fine earlier in the titration.
questions.modelAnswer: Because the colour change at the endpoint is sharp: a whole portion run in past the endpoint would overshoot and spoil the titre, so drop-by-drop addition stops the first permanent change from being missed.

questions.stem: Titre 1 reads 14.90 cm3 and Titre 2 reads 15.00 cm3. State whether the two results may be averaged, and justify the decision with the concordance rule.
questions.modelAnswer: Yes: they differ by only 0.10 cm3, which is within the 0.1 cm3 concordance window, so the two results are concordant and may be averaged.
